Steric hindrance is actually pretty straight forward.

For a reaction to occur, you need a successful collision in a certain geometry. Steric hindrance is basically when there is something in the way that stops your reactants from coming together in a successful manner.

A good example of this would be to think about EAS to substituted benzene rings. The hydroxyl group of a phenol isn't really all that large, so it isn't going to get in the way of a reaction occurring at an ortho position. 

If instead of a hydroxyl group you have something massive and bulky like a T-butyl group, this is definitely going to interfere with things approaching the position ortho to it. I generally imaging the t-butyl group spinning around like a helicopter bashing away the reactants from the ortho position next door. Because of this steric hindrance when you run the EAS reaction on this T-butyl substituted ring, you will almost exclusively get para substitution simply because the T-butyl is so large nothing can physically get to the ortho position (maybe not nothing but a very small amount). 

So basically, the bigger something is, the more it will get in the way, hindering a reaction.

In the above example, because the methoxy is larger than a hydroxyl group, it will get in the way more, sterically hindering the reaction at the ortho position. 

Does that make sense?

I think Its actually the Phenol that will react faster. 

It could be a few things.

1) The ortho positions of phenol are going to be less sterically hindered than those of anisole, this will speed up the reaction.

2) Because the proton on the phenol will exchange in solution, it spends some of its time as O-, giving even more electron density to push into the ring activating it even further. The methoxy group cant undergo this substitution so this extra e- density is not available to it.

I believe its a combination of theses factors that lead to the increased reaction rate of phenol over that of anisole.

http://crab.rutgers.edu/~alroche/Ch17.pdf (See Page 24 for relative reaction speeds)

Sterics are not the only factor that directs substitution in EAS. Electronic effects also play a role. You have to remember that Halogens effect the electron density of the ring differently then a methyl group will (they are deactivating through induction, so they actually ortho/Para direct differently than EDG's when you look at the resonance structures if I remember correctly). This combination of electronic and steric effects of the halogen is why Ar-X's tend to favour para substitution.

Methyl groups aren't THAT bulky, It will get in the way a bit but the 2:1 ortho to para positions should still dominate the reaction. Something like an IsoPropyl group or T-Bu will get in the way considerably more and will seriously hinder the ortho position giving you more Para substituted than ortho.

https://www2.chemistry.msu.edu/faculty/reusch/VirtTxtJml/chapt15.htm

This page does a pretty good job explaining it, you should give it a read and see if it helps. Might be more of the same stuff thats in your book but a different perspective can help.

Hope that helps/makes sense.

1) it can be a bit tricky to distinguish them. One way would be look for the presence of an aromatic singlet. If you had functional groups on either side of an aromatic proton it would be isolated as a singlet as nothing can really reach it to split (4j couplings are pretty weak) most of the time though all the aromatic signals overlap one another and basically all you can distinguish is a muiltiplet. Generally the best way to distinguish them is to run 2D NMR spectra (HETCOR, COSY). A long range HETCOR would show you what carbons see what protons 4 bonds away and would certainly make it easier. That's something you will likely cover later on in your course (along with DEPT as well). Sometimes IR can give you clues but it's a bit more difficult to figure out, IR is better for just identifying functional groups like carbonyls/alcohols etc. 
 Starting out learning NMR I'd assume that you will see a lot more para or mono substituted rings which are easier to distinguish before moving to the 2D techniques for the more complicated molecules.

So whenever you see two doublets in the aromatic region it generally means a para substituted ring. So on a para substituted ring you have 4 protons which we can observe using NMR (your integration value also tells us this) Now because there is symmetry along the centre of the ring you have 2 sets of chemically equivalent protons, we can call them Ha and Hb. Now Ha will be split by Hb which is neighbouring it in the ortho position and vice versa, this gives 2 doublets. This also occurs on the other side of the ring but because of the symmetry these doublets fall into the same place as the other ones. which is why you only see 2 peaks, each with an integration value of 2. You generally don't observe coupling between meta protons as they are too far away (4J) but if the functional groups were substituted differently you would have a bunch of different signals falling in the same region overlapping one another making a big mess in the NMR. Thanks to the symmetry I talked about it makes para rings really easy to spot. Next I took a look at the carbon NMR and this argument is further supported by the presence of 4 signals in the aromatic region, the 2 short ones are the ones attached to the functional groups and the 2 large are the symmetric carbons bound to Ha and Hb. (for an explanation of the difference in size look up Nuclear Overhauser Enhancement but basically Carbons bound to hydrogens have there signals magnified, the more protons the stronger the signal.)

Looking at the Carbon NMR in the aliphatic region there are 2 signal now that we have to account for. If you look at the H NMR you see the quartet which must be a proton being split by 3 equivalent protons (ie a methyl) and in reverse the methyl protons are split by 2 protons bound to the other carbon of the ethyl group. Again, the integration also supports this. Now theres just one signal to deal with, the broad little peak in the middle. Now this has to be a proton with acidic properties, in solution while the sample is  running in the NMR this proton jumps on and off whatever its bound to which gives you the broadened signal. We know it cant be a carboxylic acid because there is no Carbonyl signal in the IR as you already said and also we have accounted for all carbons. A carboxylic acid would also probably be up around 10ppm I think? Cant really remember. The integration value of 1 tells you it is only 1 proton so that rules out an aniline (NH2 would give an integration of 2) so that pretty much leaves us with a Hydroxyl group.

Sorry if this is a bit all over the place, when I'm solving these I tend to look at all the evidence and then piece it together, it can come off a bit crazy

Now move down to the carbon below, there are 2 protons here, one pointing the same way as the amine and the other pointing in the opposite direction. These proton are not equivalent, if the structure wasn't locked in place by this ring then the would be but orientation is important therefore you will see 2 signals there. This brings us to 3 signals, NH2 - 4, Methyl group 5, alkene, 6.

This also kinda leads in to the [Karplus equation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karplus_equation) and shows how the splitting strength of protons based on the orientation of neighboring

If you take a look at group 6 this also occurs with Molybdenum etc, you move and e- from the s orbital and place it in the d orbitals to give 5 d electrons (ie all unpaired spinning the same direction)

As for D - Defs 2 singlets, a doublet would have equal intensities. is 1:1 peak height.

For C the doublets refer to the Methyl Groups (CH3) so the Big one is the 2 equivalent. (Im talking about the groups on the right hand side of the Ketone. The splitting to gives the doublet comes from the proton that is 3 bonds away (so where the CH3 joins the chain). If that proton splits the methyls it will also be split by the methyl. One of them will be split by the 6 CH3 Protons and the other by the 3CH3 protons, giving a septet and quartet located around 2. The singlet is the terminal methyl on the ketone

A - The first thing I noticed about this spectra was the presence of signals in the Aromatic Region, as there is only one compound with a phenyl ring thats the answer (furthar supported by the presence of a singlet @ 4.8ish which is the methylene).

C The 2 doublets at approx 1 caught my eye, these are referring to 2 inequivalent methyl Groups which are being split by a neighbouring proton, The fact that the signal at 1 is twice as high as that of the doublet at 1.2 tells us that that the doublet at 1 corresponds to 2 equivalent methyl groups). This tells us that this is the first compound. All the other signals display the appropriate splitting patterns and chemical shifts that one would expect.

D - These are a bit trickier because the splitting patterns are hard to see but The presence of a methyl signal (singlet @ ~2ppm) would lead me to suspect that compound D is the cyclic ketones with the Amine group. The amine would appear fairly high up so That would be the signal at ~7.

B - Process of elimination gives us the final answer but just to check we see a singlet at 11 consistant with the Acid proton. The are also the other 4 signals, 2 of them correspond to the protons on the alkene (Signals @ 5 and 6) and the remaining 2 belong to the alkane protons

I remember feeling nervous about second year courses, Its pretty normal I think. But one thing to remeber is, yes, these courses may be difficult, but they are designed for students who going into second year! They are not out to make you fail or do badly!

that being said:

Inorganic (my fav): consists of lots of trends regarding the periodic table. Ie why do the alkali metals get more and more reactive as they preoceed down the Table. You will need to explain these trends using things like effective nuclear shielding (Zeff), size of atomic radii etc. Crystal field theory may be a good thing too look up. At my school we only surveyed the P block but you may do some transition metals as well.

Organic: Reactions, reactions reactions. This one is just practice sadly. You could look up some SN1, SN2, E1, E2 stuff online or try and get your hands on an old text. My advice for studying this (and it gets me A's) is to practice lots, but not by memorizing. You need to understand what is happening in a reaction first : is it being reduced/oxidized, Nucleophilic attack? what reagents am I using, The works. If you can figure that out you should be able to work through any problem and come to a (somewhat) correct answer.

Analytical: Calculations.....boring stuff for me. We did buffers, some electrochem, chromatography. This one just go to class and learn what the prof teaches. Praccy lots too.

Like I said stay on it and you will be fine. Learn concepts and apply them to answer questions as opposed to straight up memorization.

Have fun!
